definition: Philip K. Dick's use of and writing about drugs: prescribed and street amphetamines from the early 1950s to 1972; LSD on two or three occasions from 1964 and one large dose of mescaline in 1970; a month at the X-Kalay rehabilitation house in 1972; the sodium pentothal and vitamins around February–March 1974; and the drugs of his fiction — Can-D and Chew-Z, JJ-180, Substance D.
pkd_relevance: Amphetamines paced the writing of the 1950s and 1960s, by Dick's own account; LSD shaped his reputation more than his work; A Scanner Darkly records the drug culture of 1970–72; and in the Exegesis intoxication becomes a model of the human condition and a candidate cause of 2-3-74.
in_the_fiction: Now Wait for Last Year (JJ-180), The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch (Can-D, Chew-Z), A Scanner Darkly (Substance D), VALIS (the Bay Area of 1971). In each, a drug hands control of the user's reality to someone else. Characters speaking, not Dick.
in_the_exegesis: 1975–80: pentothal and vitamins as disinhibitors; LSD below eternity; Allegro's sacred mushroom and Dionysian intoxication; the 'speed-self' that collapsed in 1974; A Scanner Darkly reread as a picture of a drugged mankind.
intellectual_background: Mid-century amphetamine prescribing; the psychedelic literature (Huxley, Hofmann, Leary); orthomolecular psychiatry and split-brain research (Ross, Ornstein, Bogen); Synanon-model rehabilitation; Allegro's The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross.
scholarly_debate: How much of Dick's paranoia was amphetamine psychosis (Arnold) and how much of the fiction owes to drugs at all (Rickman); the chronology of use during the Point Reyes marriage (Anne R. Dick against Arnold); the count and date of the LSD trips (Sutin, Anne R. Dick, Rickman).
chronology_summary: c. 1952: first Semoxydrine. 1958–64: two a day at Point Reyes. 1964: recreational amphetamine; first LSD. 1964–70: pills from several doctors. May 1970: mescaline, Flow My Tears. 1970–72: the Santa Venetia house; a thousand tablets a week. March 1972: Vancouver, X-Kalay. 1973: A Scanner Darkly finished. February–March 1974: pentothal, vitamins, 2-3-74. 1976: 'I take no drugs now at all.' 1977: speed for Metz. 1978–80: the Exegesis on intoxication. 1982: marijuana bought and flushed.
contradictions_summary: Twenty, kept rather than resolved: four between biographers (Point Reyes doses, LSD count, sobriety after 1972, paranoia's cause), others between Dick and his biographers and witnesses (the LSD date, Palmer Eldritch and LSD, the 1963 vision), and Dick against himself (LSD's influence, 2-3-74 and drugs, A Scanner Darkly's subject, X-Kalay).
editorial_notes: Every passage was chosen by reading it, from a sweep of the whole corpus with scripts/research/sweep_corpus.py --profile drugs. The lexicon topic Amphetamine Use, which matched the word 'speed', was not used. Fiction is lane A; the Exegesis lane B; criticism lane C; biography lane D; letters, interviews and A Scanner Darkly's Author's Note lane E.
open_questions: What drugs, if any, preceded the 1963 vision of Palmer Eldritch? — raised under Palmer Eldritch. Dick denied any; Sutin cites contemporary mentions of 'certain chemicals'. Resolvable by: the 1963–64 letters themselves, which Sutin cites but this archive does not hold.
When was the first LSD trip, and how many were there? — raised under LSD and mescaline. 1964 or 1967; one, two or three. Resolvable by: Ray Nelson's and Jack Newkom's own accounts.

What does Anthony Peake say? — raised in the cautions. His biography is catalogued but its text is not in the archive, so the portal's older description of his position cannot be checked. Resolvable by: ingesting the book.

Did Dick take amphetamines after 1972? — raised under After 1972. Sutin says once, in 1977; Arnold reports unnamed sources who say he was still abusing them in 1974. Resolvable by: Arnold's sources, which the passage does not name.
How long was the X-Kalay stay? — a month (Dick), three weeks (Sutin), or to March (Arnold). Resolvable by: X-Kalay's records, or dated letters from March–April 1972.
Which passage of A Maze of Death is the LSD vision? — Dick names the novel; Sutin quotes a 1974 letter identifying it, which this archive does not hold. Resolvable by: that letter.
What is the drug in Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said? — the novel's text is not in the archive, so the page cannot quote it. Resolvable by: ingesting the novel.

dossier_sections.heading: Drugs in Philip K. Dick
body: Few subjects attract more legend in Philip K. Dick's life than drugs, and few are better documented by Dick himself. He wrote about his pills to friends while he was taking them {{DRG-LET-1964-BROCHURE}}, explained them to interviewers once he had stopped {{DRG-INT-1979-AMPH}}, built three novels around invented drugs, and in the Exegesis made intoxication a model of the human condition {{DRG-EX-1978-OCCLUSION}}. He also contradicted himself, and his biographers contradict one another.

This page keeps those voices apart. It separates what Dick said about his own use (letters and interviews, lane E), what he theorised about it afterwards (the Exegesis, lane B), what his characters say (fiction, lane A), and what the biographers and critics conclude (lanes D and C). Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is recorded below as a contradiction, not settled.

The essay runs roughly in order, from the first Semoxydrine around 1952 to the last interview in 1982. The index underneath runs the other way: pick a substance, a novel, a theme or a biographer and see every passage that turns on it. Every bracketed reference opens the card it cites. Two caveats about the archive itself: the texts of The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch and Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said are not in it, so those novels appear only through Dick's comments and criticism; and Anthony Peake's biography is catalogued but its text is not, so his position is not represented.

dossier_sections.heading: Twenty years of speed
body: Dick's own account begins with a cure. Writing to Anthony Boucher in 1962 about the agoraphobia that had closed in on him since adolescence, he says that at twenty-four — around 1952–53 — he found a stimulant he spells semoxydrene, and that the first 5 mg cleared away the cobwebs from his brain {{DRG-LET-1962-SEMOX}}. The same letter has the "little green pills" first rescue him and then deliver him to a disastrous move. Kyle Arnold pushes the story back further, to an asthma medicine taken at six {{DRG-BIO-ARNOLD-EPHEDRINE}}.

By 1964 the cure was a supply. In September he complains that his amphetamines have dried up despite two open prescriptions {{DRG-LET-1964-SUPPLY}}; in October a forgotten brochure tells him that semoxydrine hydrochloride is methamphetamine, and that he is on the strongest dose, six a day {{DRG-LET-1964-BROCHURE}}. By November 1970, in the house in Santa Venetia, he boasts of having taken a thousand methamphetamine tablets in two weeks {{DRG-LET-1970-THOUSAND}}.

He gave two reasons, sometimes in the same breath. To a student in 1976: the amphetamines were prescribed for depression, used for about eighteen years, and taken for energy because he was paid so little per book {{DRG-LET-1976-BOGGS}}. To Charles Platt in 1979, only the second reason: sixteen novels in five years, sixty pages a day, and amphetamines the only way to do it {{DRG-INT-1979-AMPH}}.

In the Exegesis the speed becomes part of the metaphysics. Around 1979 Dick reverses the usual story of 1974: he did not go mad then but sobered up, having gone mad in the 1950s or 1960s, "perhaps due to the speed" {{DRG-EX-1979-SPEEDSELF}}. Elsewhere decades of amphetamines have speeded up his internal clock until only timeless forms were visible {{DRG-EX-1978-FASTER}}, and a list of what drove him mad puts drugs second of three, between Nancy leaving and "endogenous psychosis" {{DRG-EX-1978-DRIVENMAD}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Two trips, or three: LSD and mescaline
body: Against his reputation, Dick's psychedelic record is short. He told Platt he took LSD twice, the second dose perhaps not acid at all; the first, Sandoz acid split with a friend, sent him "straight to hell" — a frozen landscape, God judging him, Latin — and "That was in 1964" {{DRG-INT-1979-TWICE}}. He had already dated it to 1964 in a letter of 1975, calling it a "head trip" unlike the events of 1974 {{DRG-LET-1975-HEADTRIP}}. The frozen landscape recurs in his letters {{DRG-LET-1977-ICE}}, the Latin and the Roman setting in a fanzine piece of 1967 that compares LSD with a psychotic episode and with the Bardo Thodol {{DRG-LET-1967-PSYCHOSIS}}.

The witnesses do not agree on the count. Sutin has "at least two occasions" in 1964, one with Ray Nelson {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-ACID}}; Anne R. Dick tells the Nelson trip as the only one {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-ONCE}}; Gregg Rickman says two or three times and not until about 1967 {{DRG-SCH-RICKMAN-FACTS}}. Dick himself helped the legend along — he quoted Oui's claim that he had experimented with LSD since the early fifties to his publisher as a selling point {{DRG-LET-1976-OUI}}, and confessed to Vertex that he had written his own blurbs about hallucinogens {{DRG-INT-1974-ACID}}.

Did LSD affect the work? In 1973 his answer was "none at all" {{DRG-LET-1973-VERTEX}}; in 1976 he allowed one exception, a passage of A Maze of Death drawn from his first trip {{DRG-LET-1976-MAZE}}. By 1978 the verdict is moral: "There's nothing good about drugs" {{DRG-INT-1978-AQUARIAN}}.

Mescaline is the one drug Dick credited with something good. One large dose in May 1970 gave him what acid never had, an overpowering love for other people, and he put it into Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said {{DRG-LET-1970-MESCALIN}}. In the Exegesis the same dose marks the moment a "fugal" personality took over {{DRG-EX-1978-DRIVENMAD}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Palmer Eldritch: the LSD novel written without LSD
body: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, written in 1964, was read as Dick's acid novel from the start. Its drugs are Can-D, which lets Martian colonists inhabit the doll-world of Perky Pat, and Chew-Z, which delivers them instead into Eldritch's world {{DRG-SCH-BUTLER-ELDRITCH}}; Fredric Jameson reads it as one of Dick's reversals, in which the hallucination, not reality, is degraded {{DRG-SCH-JAMESON-CHEWZ}}.

Dick's account of its origin is consistent on one point: the novel came first. The face with slotted eyes was a vision of 1963, seen "before I had seen any LSD, much less taken any", which his first LSD trip then confirmed {{DRG-LET-1969-ELDRITCH}}. In 1974 he told Vertex he had written the book from reading about LSD's discovery {{DRG-INT-1974-BEFORE}}, and an English journalist that he was on no drug at the time of the vision {{DRG-INT-1974-CONTROL}}. In 1979 the reading was "an article by Aldous Huxley" {{DRG-INT-1979-HUXLEY}}; Anne R. Dick, who lived with him while he wrote it, says it was reading about hallucinogenic mushrooms {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-MUSHROOMS}}.

Other evidence pulls the other way. In 1967 Dick called the novel "a 'trip' book" and set its vision beside a second encounter "under LSD" {{DRG-LET-1967-TRIPBOOK}}. Sutin notes that at the time Dick described the 1963 vision as following "certain chemicals" and "psychedelic drugs" — not LSD, but perhaps amphetamines {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-1963}}. And Harlan Ellison recalls that Dick assured him both Palmer Eldritch and "Faith of Our Fathers" were LSD-inspired; Sutin believes Dick's later denial {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-ELLISON}}.
By 1976 Dick had a third reading of his own: the novel is not about drugs at all, but about transubstantiation, and Chew-Z is a eucharist {{DRG-EX-1976-TRANSUB}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Santa Venetia, 1970–1972
body: The worst years are the best attested, because so many people were in the house. In the late sixties, Sutin writes, acid, pot and hash held no special fascination for Dick, but pills did, from a rotating set of doctors {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-PILLS}}; Nancy Hackett told Anne R. Dick it came to seventy a day {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-SEVENTY}}. After Nancy left in September 1970 the Santa Venetia house filled with young users, and the pills became jars of a thousand street white crosses {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-PARANOIA}}. Cindy, one of the teenagers, remembered a thousand "beans" a week — and that Phil would not touch pot {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-POT}}.

In the spring of 1971 Dick told a psychiatrist at Stanford the same figure, a thousand Methedrine tablets a week {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-STANFORD}}; later that year his own psychiatrist, seeing no withdrawal, thought him a hypochondriac {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-DRA}}. Sutin, describing the paranoia of those months, refuses to choose between the real dangers of the house and the known effects of the drug {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-PARANOIA}}.

Dick's fiction of the period's end is VALIS, which opens in 1971 with a friend phoning Horselover Fat for Nembutals to kill herself; Fat does uppers, not sleeping pills {{DRG-FIC-VALIS-UPPERS}}. The narrator's verdict on the Bay Area of the sixties is that it was like a plague, and no one could tell how much was drugs {{DRG-FIC-VALIS-PLAGUE}}. In a letter of 1981 Dick remembers a junky from those years as the most humane person he had known {{DRG-LET-1981-JUNKY}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Vancouver and X-Kalay
body: In February 1972 Dick went to Vancouver as a convention guest of honour and stayed. After a suicide attempt in March, a crisis line sent him to X-Kalay, a residential community run on Synanon lines for heroin addicts out of Canadian prisons. From inside it he wrote, "I owe my life to them" {{DRG-LET-1972-XKALAY}}. What he saw there — addicts who looked twice their age, a girl addicted at fourteen — made him an enemy of drugs and dealers {{DRG-LET-1972-HEROIN}}. That summer he named marijuana, hashish and LSD as causes of his wife's breakdowns, and so of his own collapse; his amphetamines are not on the list {{DRG-LET-1972-LINDA}}. On Los Angeles radio he refused to concede that good acid was fine {{DRG-LET-1973-RADIO}}.

He told Gillespie he spent a month there {{DRG-LET-1972-HEROIN}}; Sutin says three weeks, and that Dick, who had told Vertex he posed as a heroin addict to get in, never touched heroin {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-THREEWEEKS}}. Sutin credits X-Kalay with ending his regular use of speed after nearly twenty years {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-NEVERAGAIN}}.

Dick's own verdict changed. In 1975 he decided its education had been faulty — it had taught him that the individual alone is doomed {{DRG-LET-1975-FAULTY}}. In the Exegesis the Synanon game he had played there becomes "the exact analog of CP brainwashing" {{DRG-EX-1977-SYNANON}}, and in A Scanner Darkly the rehabilitation centre grows the drug {{DRG-FIC-SCANNER-FIELD}}.

dossier_sections.heading: A Scanner Darkly
body: A Scanner Darkly was finished in the spring of 1973, the week his ex-wife wrote that street drugs had caused her breakdowns {{DRG-LET-1973-NANCY}}, and published in 1977. Its drug is Substance D — dumbness, despair, desertion, and finally "Slow Death", as the undercover agent Fred says in a speech that gives him away {{DRG-FIC-SCANNER-SLOWDEATH}}. It opens with Jerry Fabin washing invisible aphids out of his hair {{DRG-FIC-SCANNER-BUGS}}; it gives the split between Fred and the man he watches, Bob Arctor, a neurology — competing hemispheres {{DRG-FIC-SCANNER-HEMISPHERES}}; and it ends in a field of blue flowers grown by the rehabilitation centre itself {{DRG-FIC-SCANNER-FIELD}}.

Dick never quite decided whether the book was research or memoir. Joking to a radio friend in 1973, he presented his years in the subculture as research — "I even had to (ugh) partake of dope" {{DRG-LET-1973-RESEARCH}}. The Author's Note says the opposite, in his most quoted lines on the subject: drug misuse is "not a disease, it is a decision" {{DRG-NOTE-SCANNER-DECISION}}, and he is on the list of the dead and damaged, "not a character in this novel; I am the novel" {{DRG-NOTE-SCANNER-NOVEL}}. To others he called it a roll call of his friends {{DRG-LET-1975-ROLLCALL}}, every character a real doper {{DRG-LET-1977-DOPERS}}, written to record them and to attack drugs {{DRG-INT-1981-RECORD}}.

In the Exegesis the novel keeps changing subject. Readers assume the government makes Substance D, and Dick and K. W. Jeter agree this can be inferred {{DRG-EX-1977-SLAVE}}; the Author's Note's "punished entirely too much" comes to mean the work camp, not the drug {{DRG-EX-1977-NOTE}}; the book is about the punishment for playing instead of toiling, "not drugs" {{DRG-EX-1978-PLAYING}}. Yet by 1978–80 nothing in his work outweighs its study of brain damage {{DRG-EX-1978-IMPAIRMENT}}, and Jeter's line — that the dopers on Substance D alone understood the reality situation — becomes a key {{DRG-EX-1978-JETER}}.

dossier_sections.heading: JJ-180, Can-D and the others
body: Dick's invented drugs share a structure. JJ-180, in Now Wait for Last Year (1966), addicts after a single dose and is supplied by an ally in a war to the people it is used to control: "that's why we put you on it" {{DRG-FIC-NOWWAIT-ADDICT}}. The party where it is passed round includes a wealthy author on mysticism for whom every new hallucinogen is "allied with religion" {{DRG-FIC-NOWWAIT-HASTINGS}}. Can-D and Chew-Z are sold by competitors; Substance D is grown by the rehabilitation centre. In each, a chemical gives someone else control of what the user takes to be real.

Dick noticed the pattern himself. Around 1978 he lays Palmer Eldritch, A Maze of Death and A Scanner Darkly side by side as one diagnosis: a perception "deliberately induced by a drug or drug-like substance" that cannot test reality {{DRG-EX-1978-OCCLUSION}}. The VALIS he planned in 1977 had a character named Phil take STP to see the god, and fear that anything he saw would be put down to the drug {{DRG-LET-1977-STP}}; the VALIS he published begins instead with a death from LSD {{DRG-LET-1979-VALIS}}.

dossier_sections.heading: 1974: pentothal, vitamins, lithium
body: The experiences of February and March 1974 had chemical neighbours, and Dick listed them himself. In February he was given sodium pentothal for a wisdom-tooth extraction. In the following weeks he took the "orthomolecular" water-soluble vitamins, on purpose: he had read Robert Ornstein on the right hemisphere, had just written a novel about drug-damaged brains, and set out to switch his own right hemisphere on {{DRG-LET-1975-SPLITBRAIN}} {{DRG-LET-1975-ORNSTEIN}} {{DRG-LET-1977-JAYNES}}. Sutin traces the formula to a Psychology Today article {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-VITAMINS}}.

The vitamins and the pentothal appear in nearly every causal account Dick gave. The vitamin C overdose was "crucial" for neural firing, and pentothal is the "truth drug" {{DRG-EX-1975-VITAMINC}}; the pentothal and the girl with the fish necklace were "necessary causal agents" {{DRG-EX-1975-CAUSAL}}; to his mother he lists the pentothal, the vitamin C and the girl together {{DRG-LET-1976-PENTATHOL}}. Later lists add lithium {{DRG-EX-1978-FLUSHING}}, and a political version in which a friend had predicted that pentothal would release a dissociated self {{DRG-EX-1978-HAL}}. Arnold adds Percodan, a diuretic and psychiatric drugs, and reports claims that Dick was still taking amphetamines {{DRG-BIO-ARNOLD-COVERT}}.

What Dick never says is that the chemicals made the experience. They released it, disinhibited it, or prepared the ground. In February 1981 he insists that when the first-century world broke through he was no longer under the pentothal {{DRG-LET-1981-NOLONGER}}; six months later the pentothal is how he got in touch with his unconscious {{DRG-LET-1981-UNCONSCIOUS}}. In 1975 he conceded that a later vision was "a mescaline type of experience" and that he was "loaded", then denied that this explained it {{DRG-LET-1975-LOADED}}; by 1977 the mescaline-like agent was a toxin secreted by his own brain {{DRG-EX-1977-TOXIN}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Intoxication as theology
body: In the Exegesis the vocabulary of drugs becomes religious. The pentothal stood in for the trance of the ancient mysteries, "perhaps even drug induced" {{DRG-EX-1975-MYSTERIES}}. John Allegro, who derived Christianity from a mushroom cult, was "partially correct" {{DRG-EX-1976-ALLEGRO}}, and Dick's own psychedelic experience may have "paved the way" {{DRG-EX-1976-PAVED}}. LSD reaches one kind of altered time but not eternity, which he reached only in 2-3-74 {{DRG-EX-1978-THREESTATES}}.

The positions are not consistent. In one entry he was intoxicated in 1974, but "not by LSD - it wasn't a flash-back": by Valis, and Dionysos smuggled the secret to us {{DRG-EX-1978-NOTLSD}}. In another he crossed into the other world "as I had taken a pscyhedelic" — a sentence that may mean "as if" {{DRG-EX-1978-MUSHROOM}}. In a third, the plasmate needs the sacred mushroom as catalyst, and "the drugs I took reacted to the plasmate in me" {{DRG-EX-1978-INGREDIENTS}}. Throughout, mankind is "drugged" and asleep, and Substance D is a picture of the human condition {{DRG-EX-1978-JETER}}.

Outside the notebooks, Tim Powers remembered a night in March 1979 when Dick, having smoked some marijuana, demanded to see God and saw the Ark of the Covenant — though his visions, Powers adds, were "generally not dope-related" {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-ARK}}.

dossier_sections.heading: After 1972: sober, mostly
body: In September 1976 Dick wrote that he took no drugs at all and recommended them to no one {{DRG-LET-1976-BOGGS}}. A year later, nervous about flying to the Metz festival, he scored a supply of speed — the only time in his last decade, Sutin says {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-METZ}}. Around 1978 he counts among his blessings that he is "no longer abusing drugs, legal or illegal" {{DRG-EX-1978-NOLONGER}}. Doris Sauter remembered no amphetamines, but "a little grass, a little coke" {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-DORIS}}; and in his last interview Dick described buying marijuana in order to flush it, because he enjoyed scoring but did not want to take it {{DRG-INT-1982-FLUSH}}.

dossier_sections.heading: What the biographers disagree about
body: Lawrence Sutin (1989) is the most detailed and the most even-handed: he gives competing witnesses and often declines to choose. On the 1950s he sets a friend's memory of regular doses against Dick's first wife Kleo's insistence that he took nothing {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-BERKELEY}}, and quotes a stepfather's note dating his use to a prescription from Kleo's father in 1951 {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-STANFORD}}. By the Point Reyes years, for Sutin, Semoxydrine was "a steady fuel for the writing" {{DRG-BIO-SUTIN-FUEL}}.

Anne R. Dick (1995), married to him from 1959 to 1964, remembers two prescribed Semoxydrine a day that she did not ask about {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-SEMOX}}, and dates recreational use to after he left her {{DRG-BIO-ANNE-RECREATIONAL}}. Kyle Arnold (2016), a clinical psychologist, reads the same marriage as a time of secret and escalating doses, and the paranoia Anne describes as amphetamine paranoia {{DRG-BIO-ARNOLD-ANNE}}.

Arnold's larger thesis is that commentators blamed "the wrong drug": not LSD but amphetamines explain Dick's paranoia {{DRG-BIO-ARNOLD-WRONGDRUG}}, and everything taken as schizophrenia was amphetamine psychosis {{DRG-BIO-ARNOLD-PSYCHOSIS}}. Gregg Rickman (1984), the first to set out the facts, concluded almost the reverse about the novels: their collapsing realities come from imagination, not from any drugs {{DRG-SCH-RICKMAN-FACTS}}. Dick himself gave three causes for his madness, of which drugs were one {{DRG-EX-1978-DRIVENMAD}}.

They also disagree on smaller facts: how many LSD trips, and when; whether regular speed ended in 1972; how long he stayed at X-Kalay. Each is listed under Contradictions below with the passages on both sides.

dossier_sections.heading: What this page does not claim
body: It does not say which drug, if any, caused the experiences of 1974. Dick himself offered pentothal, vitamins, lithium, mescaline-like toxins and intoxication by God, often in the same year, and never said a chemical produced them.

It does not represent Anthony Peake. His A Life of Philip K. Dick (2013) is catalogued, but only its title page is in the archive, so the position attributed to him in the portal's older essay on this subject cannot be checked. The same essay mentions a temporal-lobe hypothesis in Arnold; the archive's text of Arnold does not contain one.

It does not use the lexicon-scanned topic Amphetamine Use. That topic matched the word "speed", and most of its passages concern velocity or the speed of light. Every passage here was read before it was included.

Dates for the Exegesis are those of the folder or section a passage is filed in, narrowed where the entry dates itself. Section 016 is filed under October 1978 but runs to 1980; the folder filed under September 1976 runs to 1979.

mention_cards.context: A long autobiographical letter about agoraphobia. Dick says that at twenty-four — around 1952–53 — two things pulled him out of a closing-in world: teaching himself to drive, and a stimulant he spells semoxydrene. The first 5 mg, he writes, gave back the clarity he had been losing for fifteen years and let him see the delusion he had been living in. Later in the letter the "little green pills" save him and then deliver him to a disastrous move. The earliest dated account of his amphetamine use in the archive, and it is an account of a cure.
mention_cards.pith: the first 5 mg which I took cleared away the cobwebs from my brain
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Semoxydrine was a brand of methamphetamine hydrochloride (Dick learns this himself in October 1964: DRG-LET-1964-BROCHURE).
mention_cards.passage: … And, at nineteen, I had heard an analyst at Langley Porter tell me that without good therapy, I would be progressively more confined until at last I wouldn’t be able to stir from my room (that diagnosis given when my only fear was of large theatres, such as the War Memorial Opera House). It looked as if the black curtain was descend­ ing everywhere I looked. But then two things happened. I bought a car, and, at twenty-four, taught myself to drive. And I stumbled on a stimulant drug called semoxydrene; the first 5 mg which I took cleared away the cobwebs from my brain, restored the clarity of viewpoint which I had progressively lost over fifteen years. In that first instant, I saw—not merely clearly—but I also caught sight, lit­ erally, of the delusional viewpoint which I had been holding, as it melted away; without realizing it, I had perceived PEOPLE ALWAYS WATCHING ME. For instance, I had often stood by the …

mention_cards.context: A comic letter from Oakland, months after leaving Anne and the Point Reyes house. In among the cats and the Avon Lady, Dick complains that his amphetamines have run out despite two open prescriptions, and jokes about something injectable instead. The tone is play; the fact underneath is that by 1964 he was managing a supply.
mention_cards.pith: I don’t even know why my supply of amphetamines has dried up, and I had two open prescriptions.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … It’s late and the cats tell me that Things are not outside any more be­ cause the sun went down, and the Things (e.g. the Avon Lady) can’t venture out when the sun is down, because if they do they melt. Don’t ask me why. I don’t even know why my supply of amphetamines has dried up, and I had two open prescriptions. Time will heal that, however; I got now, you should excuse the expression, a better deal cooking anyhow. It’s injectible injectable aw fuck it; you mainline Dial soap. See, I can write a lot of short papa. Para. Yes, …

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Terry and Carol Carr, October 22, 1964
mention_cards.context: Dick reports to the Carrs that a druggist forgot to remove the brochure from his refill, so after seven years ("or is it nine?") he has finally read what his pills are: semoxydrine hydrochloride is methamphetamine. He is up to the strongest dose, six a day, and quotes the warning that overdose can cause hallucinations and death with mock horror. Sutin reprints the passage as the epigraph to his account of these years.
mention_cards.pith: I am up to six 7.5 mg of them a day, and 7.5 is their strongest dose
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.passage: … You made up that “quote” from the Nu _Yorker,_ you know you did. Also, you made up the dime “thank you” machine—inspired. (two) Well, I have an East Oakland care quotation, which is the brochure from the pills I’ve been taking for seven years (or is it nine? My mind seems oddly fuzzy somehow), semoxydrine hydrochloride, which I now learn is meth' amphetamine hydrochloride (i.e. another name for methadrine), because, see, this last refill time—I am up to six 7.5 mg of them a day, and 7.5 is their strongest dose—the druggist forgot to snatch loose the accompanying brochure, so after all these years I got to read about the side-effects, etc. of the pill. One sentence under the subtitle HUMAN TOXICITY particularly made my decade. It reads like this, gang: Overdoses, may, in addition, cause hallucinations, delirium, peripheral vascular collapse and death. (Eeg, gak, wach, fug, gugh, whuh!) …

mention_cards.context: Written for a fanzine discussion. Dick compares an eight-hour psychotic episode of a few weeks earlier — triggered, he thinks, by deaths and money troubles — with the LSD experience: the same amplified senses, the same lost time sense, a delusion that an outside force was directing him. He then proposes that the LSD trip resembles the Bardo Thodol, and recalls that his first trip put him in Rome during the Punic Wars, speaking Latin.

mention_cards.context: A long letter from the Santa Venetia house, among friends who have talked each other out of suicide. mention_cards.context: Written from inside X-Kalay. Dick tells a Swedish correspondent that after a collapse in Vancouver he tried to kill himself, that Suicide Prevention sent him to the X-Kalay Foundation, and that its regime — constant company, hard physical work, isolation from everything he knew — is rebuilding him. mention_cards.context: Dick explains to an English editor how 1974 began. Well, Mal­ colm, having the ortho-molecular vitamin formula in my possession I began exper­ imenting. . .and to compound all this, I had written the rough draft of my new novel A SCANNER DARKLY, in which I studied the drug-damaged brain and concluded that the basic impairment which I’d seen in the bumed-out members of the drug subculture which had so horrified me, had to do with “split brain” phe­ nomena of some obscure kind, and had done a vast amount of study on this, and theorizing, for the novel. I even heard it from producers and the like, here in the Hollywood area. Will Phil ever write again? It would of course cause me acute embarrassment to handle the book this way (make that embarrassment), but truth is truth. mention_cards.passage: … In the course of the novel, Phil Dick has to read Houston Paige’s notes on Zebra and listen to Nicholas Brady’s experiences with VALIS. Finally (as you already know, of course) it becomes evident to Phil (and to the reader through Phil) that Zebra and VALIS are one and the same. Phil is somewhat envious of both Nicholas and Houston; one has experiences that are extraordinary, the other has a schizophrenic theory which is extraordinary, while PKD the great writer gets only to hear about it second-hand. Thus the idea enters Phil’s head that he will turn on and possibly, via a psychedelic, be able to perceive and com­ prehend Zebra/VALIS on his own. So Phil takes a hit of STP (DOM), kicks back, hoping to see Zebra/VALIS. Here roughly is what happens. Phil once bought a little antique ikon, a little wooden statue of a Catholic cardinal with hat, robes and alb. The alb is all scratched, with flakes of paint missing; it is very old, certainly at least 150 years old, with good vibes; Phil likes to contemplate this statue, which he calls affectionately “The little saint,” because its measured calm reassures him when his head is all screwed up. This time, however, on the STP, Phil suddenly sees the flaked-off spots on the white alb of the cardinal begin to change. The spots turn into vines growing and twist­ ing together; at the same time purple clusters form here and there, amid the now­ green branches, leaves and stems. The little wooden statue, normally so serene and tranquil, all at once turns into a replica of Dionysus, represented by the tan­ gle of grape vines growing up his front. Phil (under the influence of the STP) realizes The Truth: that hiding within the Christian cardinal and hence within the Christian God is the ancient Greek god of joy and intoxication and excess. Phil imagines that rather than hallucinating he has penetrated the veil of illu­ sion, as he has always wanted to, and this is reality within: Dionysus posing as Christ, that Christ and Dionysus are one and the same. Phil knows from having read Jung that Dionysus was the “god of metamorphosis,” and Christ was noth­ ing more than a metamorphosis of Dionysus as the god passed itself along through history under first one cover-name and then another. All the Christians except the very early ones have been fooled, but, he realizes, the original Chris­ tians who actually knew Jesus were given the real story. This is the secret which they knew and passed along, but which was lost due to the persecution and mur­ der of them by the Romans. After a century or so there were no more authentic Christians any longer, and so the cover story passed into history. Naturally, Phil is elated at this discovery. Look what he knows! What fools all the billions of Christians are! Little do they know! But then he senses—rather than just hears—someone laughing behind him. Turning his head he almost sees a person who at once conceals himself. It is the great Dutch humanist and scholar Erasmus. It is Erasmus who is laughing at him—until Phil surprised him by turning around and catching a glimpse of him. (This “glimpse” phenomenon is precisely the sort of contact that Houston Paige has had with Zebra—catching the presence of motion at the periphery of his vision, but, when he turns to look, there is nothing there. Zebra has con­ cealed itself within nearby objects, utilizing its mimicry system. Thus we see in Phil’s admittedly hallucinogenic experience something resembling Houston Paige’s psychotic experience; the two are linked, and both are linked with Nich­ olas Brady’s.) “I see you,” Phil says to Erasmus. “I didn’t think you’d ever see me,” Erasmus says with chagrin. “That’s because I was sure you’d never turn on again. The STP made it possible for you to finally see me.” “Then you’re always there?” “Always. I’ve been writing your stories and novels for you all these years. And you never guessed. I even gave you a clue years ago when you were invent­ ing Swifties. Remember the one you made up that went, ‘I think I’ve got mastoid­ itis and piles, Tom said irascibly’? That was a clue. Ear—ass. Erasmus.” Erasmus chuckles. “I love puns. But you never caught on. I’ve enjoyed writing through you. You are prolific, the way I was; you just dash the stuff off without rewriting. That’s how I always did it And I was very pleased that you liked my book IN PRAISE OF FOLLY when you read it I know you share my views about the ‘Fool for Christ’” “What about Dionysus?” Phil says. “Didn’t I finally penetrate to absolute reality upon seeing Dionysus within this statue of a Christian cardinal?” “That is me,” Erasmus says, “posing as Dionysus. I was the greatest Greek scholar of the entire Renaissance. I did the first new translation of the New Testa­ ment from Greek into Latin since St. Jerome.” Erasmus laughs. Phil is disappointed. He thought he’d seen into the heart of the Christian gnosis, its most secret mystery, and here it was nothing but the spirit of Erasmus shucking him. Less stoned now, Phil puts on his headphones and listens to Bach and Pur­ cell for hours. Meanwhile, directly in front of his face (he is seated facing the wall, the way cats do) there is an 8x10 glossy of his favorite movie star, Victoria Principal. All the time that he is listening to the headphones his spaced-out mind is engramming on Victoria. At the bottom of the glossy it reads: PROPERTY OF UNIVERSAL STU­ DIOS. Phil engrams on this, too. The next day when he gets up, Phil is still stoned, but he doesn’t know it He gets the number of the publicity department at Universal and calls it From the lady there he gets the name and number of Victoria Principal’s agent, in the William Morris Agency. Pretty soon Phil is on the phone, talking to Ms. Principal’s agent Stoned to his scalp, Phil tells the agent that he, Phil, has writ­ ten a fantastic screenplay of UBIK and it is going to be produced at a cost of ten million dollars. Chuck Heston is going to play Joe Chip; Lee J. Cobb Runciter, and they—note the they—they want Ms. Principal to play Pat Conley. Phil and the agent discuss the role. Phil says it’s the largest part in the screenplay and it will make Ms. Principal immortal. The agent is polite, but he realizes that Phil is lay­ ing a hype on him, that in point of fact although Phil is who he says he is, his real motive for calling is that he is scheming on Victoria Principal and wants her phone number. Phil keeps rapping on about “The need to discuss this with Ms. Principal directly.” Agents of pretty actresses get this all day long. The agent doesn’t give him her phone number. Phil spends the rest of the day writing a rambling letter to Ms. Principal outlining all his vast achievements and importance, then mails it to her care of her agent, along with a copy of UBIK, in which he has cunningly written his own phone number on the last page of the next-to-last chapter. Two days later Phil’s mind becomes clear again, or rather relatively clear again. He realizes how stoned he was. He did not experience Zebra or VALIS; all he experienced was the invisible spirit who writes his books, Erasmus. He _thought, for_ a moment, that he was experiencing Dionysus, which might have fit­ ted in somewhere, since Dionysus is mentioned a number of times in Paige’s notes, but that was only Erasmus pretending to be Dionysus, and getting away with it because of his enormous knowledge of Greek. Phil has to reluctantly write off the experience as a failure. It is only later that realizes, very suddenly, that it might not have been true that what he experienced was Erasmus posing as Dionysus. Isn’t Dionysus, according to Jung, the god of change, of metamorphosis? Maybe it was Dionysus posing as Erasmus! In fact, that’s more likely. Dionysus was taken by surprise when Phil perceived him concealed within the garb and trappings of Christian­ ity. Dionysus doesn’t want that secret revealed to the world; he doesn’t want his cover blown. So immediately Dionysus metamorphosed once more, this time into Erasmus, and gave Phil that long song-and-dance to throw him off the track. The trouble is, Phil can’t be sure—will never know as long as he lives— which was true. Evidently he will have to write off the experience as nothing more than a hallucination. But there is one valuable outgrowth of this experience for him: he realizes the difficult problems which both Nicholas and Paige face in dealing with their respective material. Neither can be sure that there is anything there at all— that’s the first problem: it may be “all in their mind.” But if they ever get past that problem and do decide that some kind of evidence indicates that some­ thing is there, something real did happen—then they’re stuck with the near­ impossibility of formulating it. If no one else in history ever saw it, or if he did left no record of it—what a terrible ordeal, to find terminology, to escape the onus of pathology, to express what he’s experienced or thought in ways which actually communicate and are not just neologisms. Phil is relatively lucky; he can just ascribe it to the STP. But what about Nicholas? And Paige? Phil can see it clearly: Paige gets called a nut, and Nicholas a liar. The credibility of each is destroyed. And if Phil _had_ come up with anything—in his case it would be attributed to psychedelic drugs. This gives him more sympathy for both men. But of course the ultimate cri­ terion is that what Paige says and what Nicholas says dovetail independent of each other. And this is, of course, a form of verification for both.
